title: Isaiah and the prophets of the eighth century

intro.text: Amos, Hosea, Isaiah and Micah date their books by the same kings: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah, and, for Amos and Hosea, Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel.

Amos and Hosea spoke to the northern kingdom. Isaiah's word is “concerning Judah and Jerusalem”, Micah's “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem”. Their days saw Assyria come west: Pul king of Assyria took tribute from Menahem, Tiglath-pileser carried away captives, and Samaria fell in Hoshea's ninth year.
Joel's book names no king and gives no date. He is placed here, where many readers place him, and the views on his date are shown on his page.

prophets.name: Amos
prophets.title: Prophet to Israel in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam son of Joash
prophets.tagline: A herdman of Tekoa in Judah, sent to prophesy at Beth-el in the northern kingdom.

claim.text: The heading dates Amos's words “in the days of Uzziah king of Judah ... two years before the earthquake”. Scripture records no words between them.

Amos's third vision ends, “I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.” Amaziah the priest of Beth-el sent word to Jeroboam that “Amos hath conspired against thee”, reporting him as saying “Jeroboam shall die by the sword”. Scripture does not tell what Jeroboam did, and does not record Amos and the king meeting.

quote.text: I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel

claim.text: Answering Amaziah, Amos says, “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit.” The heading calls him one “among the herdmen of Tekoa”.

how.text: The book is “The words of Amos ... which he saw concerning Israel”.
Five visions are told in the first person, three of them opening “Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me”.
He prophesied at Beth-el, “the king's chapel”, and Amaziah told him to flee into Judah and prophesy there.
He says the prophet cannot keep silent: “the Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?”

claim.text: The book opens with the LORD's voice from Jerusalem and a run of oracles, “For three transgressions ... and for four”, against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon and Moab, then Judah, and last and longest Israel.

quotes.text: The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem

claim.text: Israel is charged with selling “the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes”, with taking bribes and turning aside the poor in the gate, and with false balances in the market.

quotes.text: they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes

claim.text: “I hate, I despise your feast days”: offerings and songs are refused while judgment does not flow.

quotes.text: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream

claim.text: Not Beth-el, Gilgal or Beer-sheba: “Seek ye me, and ye shall live”; “Hate the evil, and love the good”, and “it may be” the LORD will be gracious to “the remnant of Joseph”.

quotes.text: Seek good, and not evil, that ye may live

message.theme: The day of the LORD is darkness

claim.text: Those who long for the day of the LORD are warned that it is “darkness, and not light”.

quotes.text: Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light

claim.text: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Plagues had come, and five times the refrain is “yet have ye not returned unto me”.

quotes.text: prepare to meet thy God, O Israel

claim.text: The book ends with a promise: the fallen tabernacle of David raised, the captivity brought back, and Israel planted “upon their land”.

quotes.text: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen

quote.text: because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron
because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver them up to Edom

words.to: “Ye kine of Bashan” in the mountain of Samaria

quote.text: Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan, that are in the mountain of Samaria, which oppress the poor, which crush the needy
Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword

claim.text: The Lord formed grasshoppers eating the latter growth; Amos prayed “O Lord GOD, forgive”, and “The LORD repented for this”.
A fire that “devoured the great deep”; Amos prayed “cease, I beseech thee”, and “This also shall not be”.
The Lord with a plumbline: “I will not again pass by them any more.” Amos does not pray this time.
“The end is come upon my people of Israel.”
“I saw the Lord standing upon the altar”: none of them shall escape.
Nine chapters: the oracles against the nations, three “Hear this word” discourses and woes on Samaria, five visions with the clash at Beth-el set among them, and a closing promise.

James at the council: “to this agree the words of the prophets”; the wording differs from the King James Amos.

claim.text: He reported Amos to Jeroboam and told him, “O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah ... But prophesy not again any more at Beth-el”.

places.name: Tekoa
places.note: His home: “among the herdmen of Tekoa”

places.name: Beth-el
places.note: Where Amaziah sent him away; “the king's chapel”

scripture.text: Amaziah told Amos to flee to Judah and “eat bread, and prophesy there”. Amos answered with a word against Amaziah. Scripture does not say whether Amos left, or how or where he died.

tradition.text: The Lives of the Prophets, attributed to Epiphanius, tells that Amos was killed by a blow on the temple struck by Amaziah, priest of Beth-el.
tradition.who: The pseudo-Epiphanian Lives of the Prophets, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1901)
tradition.when: date of the Lives not given in the source read

tradition.text: A rabbinic tradition says King Uzziah killed Amos, striking him on the forehead with a glowing iron. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives it from Gedaliah ibn Yahya's Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah as quoted in the Seder ha-Dorot, and notes that the Venice edition of 1587 does not mention it.

tradition.when: no date given in the source read; the Jewish Encyclopedia notes that the Venice edition of 1587 lacks the story

views.label: Scripture gives only the reign
views.holders: Amos 1:1; Zechariah 14:5

argument.text: Amos's words are dated “two years before the earthquake”, and Zechariah later recalls how the people “fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah”. Neither gives a year.

views.label: At the moment Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense
views.holders: Josephus, Antiquities 9.10.4 (about AD 93)

argument.text: Retelling Chronicles' account of Uzziah's leprosy, Josephus adds that as the king went in to offer incense “a great earthquake shook the ground and a rent was made in the temple”. Chronicles does not mention an earthquake there, and Whiston's note (1737) points to Zechariah 14:5 as the likeness.

notSaid: Scripture does not say how long Amos prophesied, whether he left Beth-el when told to, or how he died.
Scripture does not tell how Jeroboam answered Amaziah's report.

prophets.name: Hosea
prophets.title: Prophet in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, and of Uzziah to Hezekiah in Judah
prophets.tagline: Told to take “a wife of whoredoms”, he gave her children names that carried the LORD's word to Israel.

claim.text: The only king of Israel the heading names. Hosea's first son is called Jezreel, “for yet a little while, and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu”. Scripture records no words between Hosea and Jeroboam.
Named in the book's heading. Scripture records no words between them.

call.label: “The beginning of the word of the LORD by Hosea”

quote.text: Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD

claim.text: The book's first command to Hosea is to marry; the marriage itself is the beginning of his word.

how.text: “The word of the LORD that came unto Hosea”.
His marriage and his children's names are part of the message.
He speaks of the LORD's way with prophets: “I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes”.

claim.text: Israel's going after Baal is told as a wife's unfaithfulness: “she said, I will go after my lovers”, not knowing that the LORD gave her corn, wine and oil.

quotes.text: For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal

claim.text: The LORD has “a controversy with the inhabitants of the land, because there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God”; priests are blamed for it.

quotes.text: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge
For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings

claim.text: “They have set up kings, but not by me”; Ephraim is “like a silly dove”, calling to Egypt and going to Assyria.

quotes.text: For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind

claim.text: “Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off”: the workman made it, “therefore it is not God”.

quotes.text: the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces

claim.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him”: the LORD taught Ephraim to walk, and cannot give him up.

quotes.text: How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel?

claim.text: The book ends with a call to return and a promise: “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely.”

quotes.text: O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity

quote.text: Hear the word of the LORD, ye children of Israel: for the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land
O Ephraim, what shall I do unto thee? O Judah, what shall I do unto thee? for your goodness is as a morning cloud
Thy calf, O Samaria, hath cast thee off
Though thou, Israel, play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend; and come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Beth-aven

claim.text: “So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim”. How the marriage is to be understood is set out under the questions.

A son named Jezreel, for the blood of Jezreel and the bow of Israel broken “in the valley of Jezreel”; a daughter Lo-ruhamah, “for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel”; a son Lo-ammi, “for ye are not my people”. Then the names are turned: “Say ye unto your brethren, Ammi; and to your sisters, Ru-hamah.”

“Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress”: Hosea bought her “for fifteen pieces of silver” and barley, and she was to abide “many days”, as Israel would abide many days without a king. The woman is not named.

word.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.”

reported.text: Matthew says the child Jesus stayed in Egypt until Herod's death, “that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Out of Egypt have I called my son.”

claim.text: Fourteen chapters: the marriage and the children (1–3), then the LORD's controversy with Israel, told in short sayings, ending with a call to return.

Mother of Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi.

scripture.text: Scripture tells nothing of Hosea's life after the book, or of his death.

tradition.text: A Jewish tradition (the Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah) says Hosea died at Babylon and that his body was carried by a camel to Safed in upper Galilee and buried there. Christian traditions make him a native of Beelmoth or Belemoth of the tribe of Issachar; Jerome, of Beth-shemesh. The Jewish Encyclopedia calls “all these stories” “historically worthless”.
tradition.who: Later Jewish and Christian traditions (the Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah; Ephraem Syrus, pseudo-Epiphanius, Jerome), as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia
tradition.when: reported 1904; the encyclopedia gives no dates for the traditions

questions.question: How is Hosea's marriage to be understood?

views.label: An event in Hosea's inner vision, not an outward marriage
views.holders: C. F. Keil (Minor Prophets, English 1868)

argument.text: Keil holds that no other course is left than to picture “Hosea's marriages as internal events, i.e., as merely carried out in that inward and spiritual intuition in which the word of God was addressed to him”; yet not as “nothing more than parables” or “poetical fictions”.

views.label: A real marriage to a woman already unchaste
views.holders: Augustine, Ambrose, Theodoret and others, and E. B. Pusey (1860), as G. A. Smith reports (1896)

argument.text: G. A. Smith reports that “a large number of other interpreters have taken the story throughout as the literal account of actual facts”, naming several Church Fathers and Pusey.

views.label: A real marriage; Gomer fell later, and Hosea saw God's purpose afterwards
views.holders: W. Robertson Smith (1882); G. A. Smith (1896)

argument.text: G. A. Smith: “She was, therefore, no dream, this woman, but flesh and blood”. Hosea's wife was pure when he married her, and he later read back God's purpose to the day of the betrothal, because the marriage was “the beginning of the word of the LORD”. He credits the view to Robertson Smith.

questions.question: Why does the heading name four kings of Judah but only one of Israel?

views.label: The heading is original: the prophets counted Judah's kings as the true kings
views.holders: C. F. Keil (Minor Prophets, English 1868)

argument.text: Keil explains the order from Hosea's own standpoint: “the prophets only recognised the legitimate rulers of the kingdom of Judah as true kings of the people of God”. Jeroboam is named as the king of Israel in whose reign Hosea began, and because of his importance for the northern kingdom.

views.label: The heading was later enlarged
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver thinks “the original title had simply ‘in the days of Jeroboam’”, and that the kings of Judah were added when the whole book needed a title, because chapters 4–14 seem to reflect the troubles after Jeroboam.

views.label: The heading's period stands, though loosely expressed
views.holders: A. H. Sayce, as reported by Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver reports that Sayce “accepts the period indicated in the title (though admitting it to be inexactly expressed)”, placing the later chapters as late as the siege of Samaria.

notSaid: Scripture does not say where Hosea lived or worked, or how he died.
Hosea 3 does not name the woman Hosea buys back; whether she is Gomer is not stated.
The “king Jareb” of Hosea 5:13 and 10:6 is not otherwise identified in Scripture.

prophets.name: Isaiah
prophets.title: Prophet in Judah in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah
prophets.tagline: He saw the Lord on a throne in the year Uzziah died, and brought the LORD's word to Ahaz and Hezekiah.

claim.text: The book's heading names Uzziah first among the kings of Isaiah's days, and Isaiah dates his vision of the Lord to “the year that king Uzziah died”. Chronicles says Isaiah wrote “the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last”. Scripture records no words between them.

quote.text: In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up

claim.text: Named in the heading of the book, and again as Ahaz's father in Isaiah 7:1. Scripture records no words between Isaiah and Jotham.

When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel came up against Jerusalem, the LORD sent Isaiah with his son Shear-jashub to meet Ahaz “at the end of the conduit of the upper pool”. Isaiah told him not to fear “these smoking firebrands” and offered him a sign “either in the depth, or in the height above”. Ahaz answered, “I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD”; Isaiah replied that “the Lord himself” would give a sign, and warned that the king of Assyria was coming. The account of Ahaz in 2 Kings 16 does not mention Isaiah.

quote.text: Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands

person.name: Hezekiah
person.note: The Assyrian siege: 2 Kings 18:13–19:37 and Isaiah 36–37, told twice

claim.text: When Sennacherib's officer stood at the upper pool, Hezekiah tore his clothes and sent Eliakim, Shebna and the elders of the priests to Isaiah, asking him to “lift up thy prayer for the remnant”. Isaiah answered, “Be not afraid”; later, after Hezekiah spread the Assyrian letter before the LORD, Isaiah sent him the LORD's answer: the king of Assyria “shall not come into this city”. Kings and Isaiah tell this in nearly the same words. Only Kings has Hezekiah's payment of three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, and Kings names three envoys (Tartan, Rabsaris and Rab-shakeh) where Isaiah names Rabshakeh alone. Chronicles, in its shorter account, says that Hezekiah and “the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz, prayed and cried to heaven”.

quote.text: He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor cast a bank against it

claim.text: Isaiah came to Hezekiah when he was “sick unto death” with the word “thou shalt die, and not live”. Hezekiah prayed and wept, and Isaiah was sent back: fifteen years would be added to his days. The two accounts differ in detail. In Kings the word comes “afore Isaiah was gone out into the middle court”, it promises that “on the third day thou shalt go up unto the house of the LORD”, the lump of figs is laid on the boil before the sign, and Hezekiah chooses that the shadow go back ten degrees, after which “Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD”. In Isaiah the sign is simply given, the figs come in two closing verses (“For Isaiah had said”), and “The writing of Hezekiah” stands between, found only there. Chronicles says only that the LORD “gave him a sign”.

quote.text: Set thine house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live

person.name: Hezekiah
person.note: The envoys from Babylon: 2 Kings 20:12–19 and Isaiah 39

claim.text: After Hezekiah showed the envoys of the king of Babylon all his treasures, Isaiah asked “What said these men?” and gave him the word that all of it “shall be carried into Babylon” and some of his sons taken. Kings names the king “Berodach-baladan”, Isaiah “Merodach-baladan”. In Kings Hezekiah answers, “Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken. And he said, Is it not good, if peace and truth be in my days?”; in Isaiah, “For there shall be peace and truth in my days”. Chronicles tells the embassy without Isaiah and says that in it “God left him, to try him”.

quote.text: Hear the word of the LORD of hosts

claim.text: Scripture records no meeting between them, but Isaiah sends Hezekiah a long word “concerning him”: “The virgin the daughter of Zion hath despised thee”, “I will put my hook in thy nose”, and “I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest”. Kings and Isaiah then tell, in nearly the same words, that the angel of the LORD smote 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, that Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, and that his sons killed him there with the sword.

Sennacherib's annals say of Hezekiah, “Himself, like a caged bird I shut up in Jerusalem his royal city”. They never claim that Jerusalem was taken, and they say nothing of a disaster to the Assyrian army (as translated by Luckenbill, 1924).

quote.text: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me

claim.text: In the year Uzziah died Isaiah saw the Lord on a throne, with seraphims crying “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts”. He cried “Woe is me! for I am undone”, and a seraph touched his lips with a live coal from the altar. Then he answered the Lord's call and was sent to a people who would hear but not understand, “Until the cities be wasted without inhabitant”.

The book does not say whether chapter 6 is Isaiah's first call. It stands after five chapters of his words, and its date, “the year that king Uzziah died”, is later than the heading's “days of Uzziah”.

how.text: The book calls itself “The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem”, and heads a later part “The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw”.
Many oracles are headed “The burden of” a city or nation: Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre and others.

He says the LORD spoke to him “with a strong hand”, and he was told to write: “Take thee a great roll, and write in it”, and again “write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come”.
He gave the word in person (to Ahaz at the conduit, to Hezekiah in his sickness), by message (“Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah”), and in sign-acts.
He spoke of disciples: “Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples.”
Chronicles names him as a writer of history: he wrote the acts of Uzziah, and Hezekiah's acts are “written in the vision of Isaiah the prophet”.

claim.text: The seraphims' cry “Holy, holy, holy” sets the tone. The name “the Holy One of Israel” comes 25 times in the King James Isaiah, 12 in chapters 1–39 and 13 in chapters 40–66, and only 6 times in the rest of the Old Testament (2 Kings 19:22, three Psalms, and twice in Jeremiah).

quotes.text: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory

claim.text: The LORD is weary of sacrifices and feasts from hands “full of blood”. He asks instead that they cease to do evil, “seek judgment, relieve the oppressed”, and offers pardon: sins “as scarlet” made “white as snow”. The song of the vineyard ends with judgment looked for, “but behold oppression”.

quotes.text: Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow

claim.text: Isaiah tells Ahaz that without belief “ye shall not be established”, and warns against going down to Egypt for help and trusting in chariots.

quotes.text: In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength: and ye would not

message.theme: Assyria the rod, and a remnant

claim.text: Assyria is “the rod of mine anger”, though its king “meaneth not so”. Yet a remnant will return: “The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God.”

quotes.text: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger

claim.text: A child is promised whose government will have no end “upon the throne of David”, and a rod “out of the stem of Jesse” on whom the spirit of the LORD rests and under whom the wolf dwells with the lamb. How these chapters are read is set out under the questions below.

quotes.text: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots

claim.text: Chapters 13–23 carry burdens against the nations around Judah, and the book looks to a day when “all nations shall flow” to the mountain of the LORD's house and learn war no more.

quotes.text: they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks

claim.text: From chapter 40 the book speaks comfort to Jerusalem, that “her iniquity is pardoned”. It mocks idols made by hand, says “beside me there is no God”, and names Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd who will say to Jerusalem, “Thou shalt be built”.

quotes.text: Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God
Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else

claim.text: The book speaks of the LORD's servant: Israel is called “my servant”, and a servant is given “for a light to the Gentiles”. In 52:13–53:12 the servant is “despised and rejected of men” and “wounded for our transgressions”. Who the servant is has been read in different ways; see the questions below.

quotes.text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed

message.theme: New heavens and a new earth

claim.text: The book ends looking to “new heavens and a new earth”, with judgment on those who have transgressed.

quotes.text: For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth

quote.text: If ye will not believe, surely ye shall not be established
Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel

claim.text: Spoken to Ahaz as “O house of David” after he refused to ask a sign.

quote.text: What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here

claim.text: Isaiah is sent to “this treasurer, even unto Shebna, which is over the house”, and told that Eliakim son of Hilkiah will be given his office.

quote.text: Be not afraid of the words that thou hast heard
The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn
I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years
all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon

words.to: The rulers and people of Jerusalem

quote.text: Hear the word of the LORD, ye rulers of Sodom; give ear unto the law of our God, ye people of Gomorrah
And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah

my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia
Howl, ye ships of Tarshish; for it is laid waste
Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden

claim.text: He saw the Lord “high and lifted up”, the seraphims above, the posts of the door moving and the house filled with smoke.
Ahaz refused to ask a sign; Isaiah gave one: a son called Immanuel, and before the child knew to refuse the evil, the land of the two kings would be forsaken.

He wrote “Maher-shalal-hash-baz” on a great roll before two witnesses; the prophetess bore a son given that name, and before the child could say “My father, and my mother” the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria would be carried off by the king of Assyria.
“Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel.”

In the year Sargon's Tartan took Ashdod, Isaiah loosed his sackcloth and shoes and walked “naked and barefoot three years” as a sign that the king of Assyria would lead away Egyptians and Ethiopians the same way.
A sign to Hezekiah in the siege: this year and next they would eat what grew of itself, and in the third year sow and reap.

signs.label: The shadow goes back ten degrees

claim.text: As a sign of Hezekiah's healing the shadow went back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz. In Kings Hezekiah chooses it and Isaiah cries to the LORD; in Isaiah the LORD gives it, and “the sun returned ten degrees”.
“Take a lump of figs”: laid on the boil, and Hezekiah recovered (Kings); Isaiah's account gives the same word in its closing verses.

word.text: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.”

reported.text: Matthew, telling of Jesus' birth: “Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet”, then the words, with “God with us”.

word.text: Light for “the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali”, “Galilee of the nations”.

reported.text: When Jesus went to live in Capernaum, Matthew says it was “That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet”.

The New Testament names “Esaias” when it quotes both halves of the book, for example John 12:38–41 (from chapters 53 and 6) and Romans 10:16, 20 (from chapters 53 and 65). Who wrote which parts is set out as views under the questions.

questions.question: Who wrote the Book of Isaiah, and especially chapters 40–66?

views.label: One book, by Isaiah son of Amoz
views.holders: J. A. Alexander (1847); G. L. Robinson (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Alexander: for two thousand years the book “was universally regarded as Isaiah's”, and its genuineness is “not a fact requiring demonstration by detailed and special proof”. Robinson writes that internal evidence “is indecisive in either case”, and points to the shared ideas of both halves, such as the name “the Holy One of Israel”, 25 times in the book and only 6 times elsewhere in the Old Testament. He adds that Ecclesiasticus (Ben Sira, which he dates about 180 BC) already praises Isaiah as the prophet who “comforted them that mourned in Zion”.

views.label: Chapters 40–66 come from a prophet near the end of the exile in Babylon
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1890); Franz Delitzsch in his last edition (1889), as reported by Robinson

argument.text: Driver: these chapters are “not the work of Isaiah” but of a prophet “writing towards the close of the Babylonian captivity”, because they address exiles in Babylon and name Cyrus as already on his way. Smith argues that in the nine places where the Gospels, Acts and Romans name Isaiah, nothing requires his name to be used “for any other end than that of reference”, so they do not settle the question. Robinson reports that Delitzsch, who had long defended the whole book, gave way in 1879–80 and in his 1889 edition took chapters 40–66, “with considerable hesitation”, as coming from the close of the exile.

views.label: Chapters 40–55 and 56–66 come from two different later writers
views.holders: B. Duhm (1892; 2nd edition 1902)

argument.text: Duhm assigned chapters 56–66 to a single later writer he called “Trito-Isaiah” (“Tritojesaia”), writing in Jerusalem shortly before Nehemiah, and the servant songs to yet another poet. Robinson (1915) reports that it had “become the fashion” to divide chapters 40–55 from 56–66, and that some critics divided the book further still.

questions.question: Who is the virgin and her son in Isaiah 7:14?

views.label: Matthew: fulfilled in the birth of Jesus
views.holders: Matthew 1:22–23

argument.text: Matthew tells Jesus' birth of Mary and says “all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child”.

views.label: Of Christ, born of a virgin
views.holders: Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 43 and 84, mid-2nd century)

argument.text: Justin argues that a true sign must be one “not common to all the first-born sons”, so the prophecy points to Christ's birth from a virgin.

views.label: A young woman, and the child Hezekiah
views.holders: Trypho and his teachers, as Justin reports them (Dialogue 43, 67, 77)

argument.text: Trypho says the Scripture reads “Behold, the young woman shall conceive”, and that “the whole prophecy refers to Hezekiah”.

views.label: A child born in Isaiah's own day: the prophet's son, or a son of Ahaz
views.holders: Ibn Ezra, Rashi (Jarchi), Gesenius and others; Kimchi and Abarbanel; as listed by J. A. Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander lists those who “suppose him to be speaking of his own wife, and the birth of his own son” (Aben Ezra, Jarchi, Gesenius and others), and Kimchi and Abarbanel, who take Immanuel to be a younger son of Ahaz. Alexander himself rejects these readings.

views.label: Of Christ, with or without a nearer sign for Ahaz
views.holders: J. A. Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander concludes that “the choice lies between the supposition of a double sense and that of a reference to Christ exclusively, but in connexion with the promise of immediate deliverance to Ahaz”.

views.label: The promised king, whose birth Isaiah expected soon
views.holders: G. A. Smith (1888)

argument.text: Smith finds it “impossible to dissociate” the child named Immanuel from the hoped-for prince of David's house, and calls Immanuel “the Messiah”; but he holds that Isaiah foretold his birth “for the near future”, and does not try to say who the mother was.

questions.question: Who is the child of Isaiah 9:6?

views.label: The Messiah, directly
views.holders: J. A. Alexander (1846); G. A. Smith (1888)

argument.text: Alexander: “The reference to Christ is not a mere typical and secondary one, but primary and positive.” Smith takes the child with the four names to be the same promised king as Immanuel.

views.label: Hezekiah
views.holders: Rashi, Kimchi, Ibn Ezra and others, as listed by Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander lists those who explained the child as Hezekiah (“Jarchi, Kimchi, Aben Ezra, Grotius, Hensler, Paulus, Gesenius, Hendewerk”), some of them by reading the titles as names of God rather than of the child.

views.label: What the New Testament does
views.holders: Matthew 4:13–16

argument.text: The New Testament quotes the verses just before (9:1–2) as fulfilled when Jesus lived in Galilee. It does not quote 9:6 itself.

views.label: Of Jesus
views.holders: Acts 8:35; Matthew 8:17; Luke 22:37; John 12:38

argument.text: When the eunuch asked “of whom speaketh the prophet this?”, Philip “began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus”.

views.label: Of the whole people of Israel
views.holders: A Jewish teacher in debate with Origen, as Origen reports (Against Celsus 1.55)

argument.text: Origen's opponent “replied, that these predictions bore reference to the whole people, regarded as one individual, and as being in a state of dispersion and suffering”.

views.label: An ideal figure drawn from Israel, which meets its fulfilment in Christ
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver calls the servant “an ideal figure, reproducing in their perfection the best and truest characteristics of the actual nation”, and adds that this figure and Isaiah's king “meet, and are fulfilled, in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ, but in the Old Testament they are distinct”.

questions.question: Which came first: 2 Kings 18–20 or Isaiah 36–39?

views.label: Isaiah wrote both
views.holders: J. A. Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Since neither text can be shown to be the original, Alexander holds “that they are both the work of the same writer, and that this writer is Isaiah”, who is recorded as a writer of the kings' history.

views.label: Kings copied from Isaiah
views.holders: Grotius and Vitringa, as reported by Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander reports “the old opinion of Grotius and Vitringa, that the narrative in Kings is a varied transcript of the one in Isaiah”.

views.label: Isaiah's chapters were taken from Kings
views.holders: Gesenius and others, as reported by Alexander (1846); S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver: “The original place of these narratives was not the Book of Isaiah, but the Book of Kings”, from which they were taken with abridgments, Hezekiah's song being added from another source; Kings has the fuller details.

views.label: Both come from an older, fuller history
views.holders: Koppe, Rosenmüller, Hitzig and others, as reported by Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander reports this view: the two are “parallel or collateral abridgments, made by different writers, from the same original”.

notSaid: Scripture does not record Isaiah's death, his age, or where he was buried.
Scripture does not name Isaiah's wife; it calls her “the prophetess” (Isaiah 8:3).
Scripture does not say whether Isaiah went on prophesying into Manasseh's reign; the book's heading ends with Hezekiah.
2 Kings 16, the account of Ahaz's reign, does not mention Isaiah.

prophets.name: Micah
prophets.title: Prophet in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah

Named in the book's heading. Scripture records no words between them.

In Jehoiakim's reign elders of the land recalled that Micah prophesied “in the days of Hezekiah” that Zion would be ploughed, and asked, “did he not fear the LORD, and besought the LORD, and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them?”

quote.text: Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death?

Against prophets who cry “Peace” for food, he says, “But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD”.
He spoke “to all the people of Judah”, as the elders remembered.

quotes.text: Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps

quotes.text: They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with iniquity

claim.text: “Prophesy ye not, say they”; the people would welcome a prophet “of wine and of strong drink”.

quotes.text: Thus saith the LORD concerning the prophets that make my people err, that bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace

quotes.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

message.theme: Who is a God like thee

claim.text: The book ends with the God who “pardoneth iniquity” and will cast sins “into the depths of the sea”.

quote.text: Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard
O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast

Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field
But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah

word.text: “Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps.”

reported.text: The elders say that Hezekiah did not put Micah to death but feared the LORD, “and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them”. They said this in Jeremiah's defence, and the chapter ends with Jeremiah not given “into the hand of the people to put him to death”.

claim.text: Seven chapters, opening with “Hear” three times: judgment on Samaria and Judah with a remnant gathered, the mountain of the LORD and the ruler from Bethlehem, and the LORD's controversy ending in pardon.

outline.title: Samaria and Judah judged; a remnant gathered

person.name: Certain of the elders of the land

claim.text: In Jeremiah's defence they quoted Micah's word that “Zion shall be plowed like a field”.

places.name: Moresheth-gath
places.note: The King James text calls him “the Morasthite”; the places data links this to Moresheth-gath of Micah 1:14

places.name: Babylon
places.note: “thou shalt go even to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered”

scripture.text: Scripture does not record Micah's death. In the reign of Jehoiakim his words were still quoted in Jerusalem.

tradition.text: Pseudo-Epiphanius makes Micah an Ephraimite and says that “for his inauspicious prophecy” he was killed by order of Ahab, thrown from a precipice, and buried at Morathi. The Jewish Encyclopedia says he is confounding Micah with Micaiah son of Imlah, who prophesied to Ahab; Micah's own heading names Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
tradition.who: The pseudo-Epiphanian Lives of the Prophets, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)
tradition.when: date of the Lives not given in the source read

questions.question: Micah 4:1–3 and Isaiah 2:2–4 are nearly the same oracle. Who first spoke it?

views.label: Isaiah took it from Micah
views.holders: J. D. Michaelis, Gesenius and others, as listed by J. A. Alexander (1846); Alexander himself leans this way

argument.text: Alexander: the passage's close tie to its context in Micah “somewhat favours the conclusion that Isaiah took the text or theme of his prediction from the younger though contemporary prophet”.

views.label: Micah took it from Isaiah
views.holders: Vitringa, Lowth and others, as listed by Alexander (1846)

argument.text: Alexander lists this as one of five views held in his day.

views.label: Both took it from an older oracle
views.holders: Koppe, Rosenmüller, De Wette and others, as listed by Alexander (1846); G. A. Smith (1896) keeps it open

argument.text: Alexander himself thinks the small differences may be “best explained” by both prophets using “a traditional prediction current among the people” or receiving it directly from the Holy Spirit. G. A. Smith thinks Micah has the more original form.

views.label: Added later to one or both books
views.holders: B. Stade, H. Hackmann and T. K. Cheyne, as reported by G. A. Smith (1896)

argument.text: Smith reports the view that the oracle was inserted by later editors in both Micah and Isaiah. He himself finds it “improbable that the same post-exilic insertion should find its way into two separate books”.

notSaid: Micah's father is not named, and Scripture does not say how he died.
Micah 1:1 calls him “the Morasthite”; Scripture does not say more about his town.
Scripture records no meeting between Micah and Isaiah, though both spoke in Hezekiah's days.

prophets.name: Joel
prophets.title: Prophet; his book names no king
prophets.tagline: He called Judah to fast after the locusts, and spoke of the Spirit poured out on all flesh.

how.text: “The word of the LORD that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.” The book gives no date and no king.
He calls the priests and the people to a fast and a solemn assembly in the house of the LORD.

claim.text: “That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten”: vines and fig trees are stripped, and the meat offering and drink offering are cut off from the house of the LORD.

quotes.text: Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation

claim.text: “The day of the LORD is at hand”: a great army, “a day of darkness and of gloominess”.

quotes.text: for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?

claim.text: The call to turn to the LORD “with all your heart”, for he is “gracious and merciful”.

quotes.text: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God

claim.text: The LORD answers: corn, wine and oil, the northern army driven off, and rain.

quotes.text: And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten

claim.text: “Afterward” the LORD will pour out his spirit on all flesh, with wonders in heaven and earth, and “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered”.

quotes.text: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

message.theme: The nations in the valley of decision

claim.text: All nations are gathered to the valley of Jehoshaphat for judgment; the Gentiles are called to “Beat your plowshares into swords”. Then Judah will dwell for ever.

quotes.text: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision: for the day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision

quote.text: Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar
Yea, and what have ye to do with me, O Tyre, and Zidon, and all the coasts of Palestine?
Egypt shall be a desolation, and Edom shall be a desolate wilderness

word.text: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.”

reported.text: On the day of Pentecost Peter says, “But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel”, and quotes the passage.

claim.text: Three chapters: the locust plague and the call to fast, the LORD's answer, the Spirit poured out, and the judgment of the nations. The book shares words with Amos: “The LORD also shall roar out of Zion” (Joel 3:16; Amos 1:2) and the mountains dropping new wine (Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13).

outline.title: Locusts, drought, and the call to fast
The LORD's answer: the years restored
The Spirit poured out on all flesh
The nations judged; Judah for ever

quotedInNT.note: Peter at Pentecost: “this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel”.
Paul, without naming Joel.

claim.text: Named only in the heading.

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Joel beyond his father's name and his book.

views.label: Early, before Amos (in the reign of Joash or soon after)
views.holders: K. A. Credner (1831), as reported by Driver (1891); E. B. Pusey (1860); A. F. Kirkpatrick (1892, “on the whole”), as reported by G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Pusey reasons that Amos opens with Joel's words (“The LORD will roar from Zion”) and ends with his promise of the mountains dropping new wine, so Joel's book was finished before Amos gathered his. Driver reports that Credner placed Joel in Joash's early reign, when the priest Jehoiada led and no king is named, and that “most scholars until recently acquiesced in his conclusion”.

views.label: After the exile, in the Persian period
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Driver: Joel names no king, no Assyria or Babylon, and no northern kingdom, and speaks of Israel “scattered among the nations”; these features “turn the balance of evidence somewhat strongly in favour of the later date”. Smith places him among the prophets of the Persian period, “writing towards 400 B.C.”.

views.label: The date cannot be proved
views.holders: Kessner (1888), as reported by G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Smith notes that Kessner “deems the date unprovable”; Driver too says the date depends “entirely upon internal evidence”.

notSaid: The book names no king and gives no date.
Scripture does not say where Joel lived, though his words centre on Zion and the house of the LORD.
Scripture does not record Joel's death; no tradition of it was found in the sources read.
